items.title: Holiday Hiring in a Cooling Labor Market: Fewer Temp Jobs, More Automation
items.body:
Every autumn, retailers, warehouses and delivery companies ramp up hiring to handle the year-end rush. This year the picture looks different. Many employers are still adding seasonal workers, but several are offering fewer temporary positions than in past years and are leaning more heavily on automation in their fulfillment centers. For job seekers, that changes where the opportunities are, how long they may last and what skills help candidates stand out.

## What Seasonal Hiring Usually Looks Like

Seasonal hiring has long been a barometer of business confidence. Retailers add cashiers, stock clerks and floor staff. Shippers and logistics firms add package handlers, drivers and sorting-center workers. Many of these roles run from roughly October through early January, and a share of them turn into permanent jobs for people who perform well.

In years when the labor market was very tight, employers competed hard for workers. They raised starting pay, offered sign-on bonuses and ran large hiring events. When hiring conditions cool, that urgency fades.

## What Is Different This Year

Several trends are shaping this year's holiday hiring season:

- **More cautious headcount plans.** Many companies are being careful about costs after a period of slower consumer spending growth and elevated borrowing costs. Rather than hiring aggressively "just in case," they are planning for expected demand and relying on existing staff for extra hours.
- **More automation in warehouses.** Robotic picking systems, automated sorting lines and conveyor technology now handle tasks that once required large temporary crews. This does not remove the need for people, but it can reduce how many short-term hires a facility needs for the same volume of orders.
- **A shift in the type of work.** Demand is moving toward roles that support automated systems, such as equipment operators, quality checkers, inventory control staff and technicians, alongside traditional hands-on handling.
- **Earlier and shorter hiring windows.** Some employers are bringing in workers earlier and for tighter periods, matching schedules more closely to forecasted peaks instead of keeping large pools on standby.
- **Greater use of existing workers.** Offering current part-time employees more hours is often cheaper and faster than onboarding new people.

Exact numbers vary by company and region, and official figures are revised over time, so it is worth checking recent releases from sources such as the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and industry groups like the National Retail Federation for the latest data.

## What This Means for Job Seekers

A cooler market does not mean there are no jobs. It means the search takes more strategy.

1. **Apply early.** Fewer openings and tighter windows mean the best shifts and locations can fill quickly.
2. **Be flexible.** Availability for nights, weekends and multiple locations makes a candidate easier to place.
3. **Highlight technology comfort.** Familiarity with handheld scanners, warehouse management software or basic equipment operation can set an applicant apart.
4. **Look beyond the obvious employers.** Grocers, restaurants, event venues, hospitality businesses and local delivery services also see holiday surges.
5. **Ask about conversion.** If you want a lasting job, ask during the interview whether seasonal staff are considered for permanent openings.
6. **Compare total compensation.** Pay rates, guaranteed hours, shift differentials, and benefits such as employee discounts or schedule flexibility can differ widely.
7. **Verify every offer.** Seasonal periods also bring job scams. Be wary of any posting that asks for payment, banking details or sensitive information before a formal offer, and apply through a company's official website.

## What It Says About the Bigger Jobs Picture

Seasonal hiring is only one piece of the labor market, but it offers a useful signal. Smaller holiday hiring plans can reflect employers' caution about consumer demand, while greater automation points to longer-term changes in how goods move from warehouse to doorstep.

Economists generally caution against reading too much into one season. Holiday hiring can be affected by the timing of promotions, weather, supply chain conditions and shifts between online and in-store shopping. A softer seasonal pattern may coincide with steady unemployment and modest job growth, a combination often described as a cooling but not collapsing labor market.

What bears watching in the coming months:

- Whether employers keep some seasonal workers on after the holidays
- How quickly job openings and hiring rates continue to move
- Wage growth, especially in retail and logistics
- Whether automation investment spreads to smaller facilities and more job categories

## The Takeaway

The holiday hiring season is still happening, but it reflects a labor market that is less frantic than in recent years and a logistics industry that is steadily becoming more automated. For workers, the best approach is to start early, stay flexible, build practical technology skills and research employers carefully. For observers of the economy, the season offers one more data point, helpful but best read alongside broader employment reports rather than on its own.

*This article is for general informational purposes only and does not constitute financial, employment or legal advice.*

items.title: The Dollar's Big Year: What a Shifting Greenback Means for Travelers, Exporters and Your Portfolio
items.body:
When the value of the U.S. dollar moves, the effects rarely stay in currency markets. They show up in the price of a hotel room in Lisbon, in a manufacturer's quarterly earnings, and in the returns on a retirement account that holds international funds. This year, the dollar has been a story in its own right. Here is a plain-language look at what tends to move the currency, and who typically benefits or loses when it does.

*This article is for general information only and is not financial, tax or investment advice.*

## What Moves the Dollar?

Exchange rates reflect the relative appeal of one currency against another. A handful of forces tend to matter most:

- **Interest rate expectations.** When investors expect U.S. interest rates to stay higher than those in other major economies, dollar-denominated assets become more attractive, and demand for the currency can rise. When the gap narrows, the opposite can happen.
- **Economic growth and data.** Strong U.S. employment, spending and inflation readings can shift expectations about central bank policy. Surprises, in either direction, often cause the sharpest moves.
- **Safe-haven demand.** In periods of global uncertainty, investors have often moved money into U.S. Treasuries, which tends to support the dollar.
- **Trade and fiscal policy.** Tariff announcements, trade negotiations and government borrowing plans can all influence how investors view the currency over time.
- **Policy in other countries.** The dollar is always quoted against something. A shift in policy at the European Central Bank, the Bank of Japan or elsewhere can move the exchange rate even if U.S. conditions are unchanged.

No single factor explains a year of currency moves. Analysts often disagree about which ones are dominant, and forecasts have a mixed track record.

## What It Means for Travelers

For Americans traveling abroad, a stronger dollar generally means more purchasing power. A euro or a yen costs fewer dollars, so meals, lodging and souvenirs can feel cheaper. A weaker dollar works the other way, nudging up the cost of the same trip.

A few practical tips:

1. **Compare the total cost, not just the headline rate.** Card fees, ATM charges and airport exchange kiosks can erase a favorable exchange rate.
2. **Pay in local currency.** When a card terminal offers to charge you in dollars, the conversion rate is often less favorable. Choosing the local currency usually costs less.
3. **Consider cards without foreign transaction fees.** These fees commonly run around 3 percent on some cards, which can add up over a long trip.
4. **Prepay big-ticket items when it suits you.** Locking in a hotel or tour price in dollars removes the exchange-rate guesswork, though it may reduce flexibility.

For visitors coming to the United States, the reverse applies: a stronger dollar makes American trips more expensive, which can affect tourism-dependent businesses and destinations.

## What It Means for Exporters and Importers

A stronger dollar makes U.S. goods more expensive for foreign buyers, which can weigh on export sales unless companies cut prices and accept thinner margins. A weaker dollar tends to help exporters by making their products cheaper abroad.

Importers see the mirror image. A stronger dollar lowers the cost of foreign-made goods and materials, which can ease costs for retailers and manufacturers that rely on imports. Consumers sometimes benefit through lower prices, though pass-through is uneven and often delayed.

There is also an accounting effect. Large multinational companies earn revenue in many currencies. When those foreign earnings are converted back into dollars, a stronger dollar shrinks the reported total, and a weaker dollar inflates it. Companies often discuss this in earnings reports as a "currency headwind" or "tailwind," and many use hedging contracts to soften the impact.

## What It Means for Your Portfolio

Currency movements matter for anyone who owns international investments, including broad funds in a workplace retirement plan.

- **International stocks and bonds.** If you hold assets priced in euros, yen or other currencies, their value in dollars depends on both the asset's performance and the exchange rate. A rising dollar can reduce returns on foreign holdings, while a falling dollar can boost them.
- **U.S. multinationals.** Companies that earn much of their revenue overseas can see profits swing with the dollar, as described above.
- **Commodities.** Many commodities, including oil and gold, are priced in dollars. A stronger dollar can make them more expensive for buyers using other currencies and sometimes puts downward pressure on prices.
- **Hedged versus unhedged funds.** Some funds use contracts to reduce currency effects. These can cost more and may behave differently from unhedged versions, so it is worth reading a fund's description.

Currency moves also tend to reverse and re-reverse over time. Many long-term investors focus on diversification and their time horizon rather than trying to predict the next shift in the exchange rate. If you are unsure how your holdings are exposed, a licensed financial professional can help you review them.

## Winners and Losers at a Glance

| | Stronger dollar | Weaker dollar |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. travelers abroad | Gain buying power | Face higher costs |
| Foreign visitors to the U.S. | Face higher costs | Gain buying power |
| U.S. exporters | Often pressured | Often helped |
| U.S. importers and shoppers | Often helped | Often pressured |
| Foreign assets held by U.S. investors | Returns may shrink | Returns may grow |

These are general tendencies, not guarantees. Real-world outcomes depend on pricing power, contracts, hedging and timing.

## The Bottom Line

The dollar's value is a moving piece in the economy that touches nearly everyone, whether or not they ever exchange a single bill. Travelers can protect their budgets by watching fees and exchange rates, businesses can plan around currency risk, and investors can understand how much of their portfolio depends on foreign currencies. Staying informed, and keeping a long-term view, is usually more useful than reacting to each day's headline.

items.title: Beef, Coffee and Cocoa: Why Some Grocery Staples Keep Setting Price Records
items.body:
Overall inflation has cooled from its peak, but anyone who has stood in a grocery aisle lately knows the headline number does not tell the whole story. A handful of everyday items, including **beef, coffee and chocolate**, have stayed stubbornly expensive. Each has its own cause, and each has a different outlook for relief.

> **Note:** This article is general background, not financial or purchasing advice. Prices vary by region, store and week, so check current figures from official sources such as the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and the USDA.

## Why averages can hide big differences

Consumer price indexes blend hundreds of goods. When energy costs ease or used-car prices fall, they can pull the overall figure down even while certain foods keep climbing. Food is also unusually exposed to things that sit outside normal economic cycles: weather, animal biology, crop disease and trade policy. That is why a few staples can keep setting records in a calmer inflation environment.

## Beef: it takes years to make more cattle

Beef prices are largely a story about **supply that cannot be rebuilt quickly**.

- **Herd size.** The U.S. cattle herd has shrunk to some of its lowest levels in decades. Several years of drought across major grazing regions pushed ranchers to sell animals early because pasture and hay were scarce or costly.
- **Biology and timing.** A heifer kept back to build the herd is not available for slaughter. It then takes roughly two years or more before her calf reaches market weight. Rebuilding therefore reduces beef supply before it increases it.
- **Costs along the chain.** Feed, fuel, labor and processing costs all affect what ends up in the meat case.
- **Trade.** The U.S. imports a meaningful amount of lean beef used in ground products. Tariffs, import limits and shifts in supplier countries can raise costs for those cuts.

**Is relief in sight?** Probably not soon. Analysts generally expect tight supplies to persist until herds rebuild, and that process can take years. Good rains and cheaper feed would help, but the lag is built into the cattle cycle.

## Coffee: a weather-driven crop in a few places

Coffee is grown in a small number of regions, so trouble in one can ripple through the global market.

- **Climate stress.** Droughts, heat and irregular rains in major producers such as Brazil and Vietnam have reduced harvests in some seasons. Arabica, the variety common in specialty drinks, is especially sensitive to temperature and rainfall.
- **Slow replanting.** A new coffee tree takes several years to bear a full crop, so losses cannot be fixed in a single season.
- **Shipping and trade costs.** Freight disruptions, currency swings and import tariffs add to what roasters pay.
- **Retail lag.** Roasters often buy ahead and use hedging contracts, so changes in the commodity price can take months to show up on shelves, in both directions.

**Is relief in sight?** It depends on harvests. Larger crops in key countries can bring wholesale prices down, but retail prices tend to fall more slowly than they rose. Shoppers may see more promotions before they see lower sticker prices.

## Cocoa: disease, weather and concentrated supply

Chocolate prices reflect one of the most concentrated supply chains in food. A large share of the world's cocoa comes from West Africa, particularly Ivory Coast and Ghana.

- **Crop problems.** Heavy rain, dry spells and plant diseases such as swollen shoot virus have cut yields in recent seasons.
- **Aging trees and thin margins.** Many farms have older trees and limited money for replanting, which holds back production.
- **Pass-through to products.** Manufacturers have responded with higher prices, smaller packages or recipe changes. Because cocoa is only one ingredient alongside sugar, dairy and packaging, the effect on a candy bar shows up with a delay.
- **Demand response.** When prices stay high, some buyers trade down or buy less, which can eventually ease pressure on the market.

**Is relief in sight?** Cocoa can swing sharply with each harvest report. A strong recovery in West African output would help, but analysts caution that retail chocolate prices usually adjust slowly even after raw cocoa falls.

## What the three have in common

| Item | Main pressure | Why relief is slow |
|---|---|---|
| Beef | Small cattle herd, drought, trade costs | Rebuilding herds takes years |
| Coffee | Weather in a few key regions, shipping | New trees need years to produce |
| Cocoa | Disease, weather, concentrated supply | Retail prices lag the raw commodity |

In each case, the problem is **supply that responds slowly**, combined with costs that tend to be passed on quickly and rolled back slowly. Economists often describe this as price stickiness: companies are quicker to raise prices than to cut them.

## Practical ways households cope

- **Shift cuts.** Ground beef, chuck and other less expensive cuts often cost less than steaks, and slow cooking makes them tender.
- **Mix proteins.** Substituting chicken, eggs, beans or lentils in some meals can lower the weekly bill.
- **Compare coffee formats.** Store brands, larger bags or whole beans ground at home can reduce cost per cup. Watch the unit price rather than the package price.
- **Buy chocolate on promotion.** Seasonal sales and store brands can offer savings, and baking chocolate can substitute for some recipes.
- **Use unit prices.** Shrinking package sizes can make a price look unchanged when it is not.

## The bottom line

Cooling overall inflation does not mean every price falls together. Beef, coffee and cocoa are held up by herds, harvests and trade costs that cannot be fixed quickly. Relief is most likely to arrive gradually, through better weather, bigger crops and rebuilt herds, and it will probably reach store shelves later than it reaches commodity markets. Until then, flexible shopping habits are the most reliable tool consumers have.
